titre: A Court Founded Never to Retry Anyone
accroche: In 1790, the Revolution creates a court tasked with quashing unlawful judgments, with an express ban on retrying the merits of cases.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the autumn of 1790, the National Constituent Assembly has to solve a problem it created itself. It has just overhauled the kingdom's judicial organization and definitively dissolved, in 1790, the parlements of the Old Regime, which had been put on vacation by a decree of November 3, 1789. It distrusts the judges who will apply the new laws: the parlements were in the habit of delaying or distorting royal laws they disliked, in the name of their right of registration. Nothing guarantees that the new courts will not do the same with the laws of the Revolution.

The answer comes in the decree of November 27 and December 1, 1790: a “tribunal de cassation” (court of cassation), established beside the Legislative Body, charged with verifying that no judgment rendered in last resort violates a procedural form prescribed on pain of nullity, or contradicts the express text of the law. Its article III sets a limit on the court with no exceptions: “Under no pretext and in no case may the court take cognizance of the merits of cases. After quashing the proceedings or the judgment, it shall remand the merits of the cases to the courts that are to hear them, as will be set out below.”

## Neither an appeals court nor a third chance

This is where the system differs from what it is often thought to be. In the 1790 scheme, a litigant who has received a judgment in last resort does not, by seeking cassation, obtain a fresh review of his file. The court annuls the proceedings or the judgment that violate the forms or expressly contravene the law, then remands the merits of the case to the courts that are to hear it. This boundary was intended from the outset, not built after the fact. It reflects the 1790 distrust of judges who were not to be allowed to reinterpret the law in their own way, but whom another court had to be allowed to rule on the facts.

The attachment to the Legislative Body marks the same distrust. The decree provides that, when a judgment has been quashed twice and a third court has ruled the same way as the first two, the question can no longer be raised before the court of cassation without having been submitted to the Legislative Body; and each year the court sends to the bar of the Legislative Body's Assembly a delegation of eight of its members, who present it with the state of the judgments rendered. The organic senatus-consultum of 28 Floréal Year XII, May 18, 1804, then gives the institution the name Cour de cassation (Court of Cassation).

## A division exported

The distinction laid down in 1790 between quashing (reviewing the law) and retrying (establishing the facts) is found beyond France. Independent since 1830, Belgium acquires a Court of Cassation in 1832, which, like the French court, does not rule on the merits. An invention born of distrust toward Old Regime judges has thus set a way of telling a supreme court from an appeals court: one reviews the law, the other retries the facts.

citation.texte: Under no pretext and in no case may the court take cognizance of the merits of cases. After quashing the proceedings or the judgment, it shall remand the merits of the cases to the courts that are to hear them, as will be set out below.
citation.source: Decree of November 27 and December 1, 1790 establishing a court of cassation, art. III

carte.punch: In 1790, a court is created with an express order never to take up the merits of cases.
carte.idee: In 1790, the Revolution creates the court of cassation with an article forbidding it to take cognizance of the merits of cases: it annuls a judgment contrary to the law, then remands the merits to the courts that are to hear them. A division that Belgium's Court of Cassation, created in 1832, also observes.

quiz.question: What can the court of cassation created in 1790 do, according to its article III?
choix: Retry the merits of the case if both parties jointly request it
Quash a judgment contrary to the law, then remand the merits to the competent courts
Itself impose a harsher sentence than the quashed judgment
Uphold or quash a judgment without having to give reasons
quiz.explication: Article III of 1790 expressly forbids the court from taking cognizance of the merits of cases: it annuls the proceedings or the judgment contrary to the law, then remands the merits to the courts that are to hear them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 1790 decree provide when a judgment has been quashed twice and a third court rules the same way as the first two?
choix: The question can no longer be raised before the court of cassation without having been submitted to the Legislative Body
The court of cassation itself decides the merits of the case
The king appoints a fourth court to retry the case
The case is definitively closed and no authority may take it up again
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article XXI of the decree provides that after two cassations and a third judgment identical to the first two, the question can no longer be raised before the court of cassation without having been submitted to the Legislative Body.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the institution created in 1790 called, before it takes the name Cour de cassation in 1804?
choix: Chamber of Requests of the King
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1790 decree creates a “tribunal de cassation”; the organic senatus-consultum of 28 Floréal Year XII, May 18, 1804, then gives it the name Cour de cassation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When does Belgium acquire a Court of Cassation that, like the French court, does not rule on the merits?
choix: In 1795, immediately after the French annexation
In 1830, at the very moment of its independence
In 1848, after the wave of European revolutions
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Independent since 1830, Belgium acquires a Court of Cassation in 1832, with Étienne de Gerlache as first president, which does not rule on the merits.
